text: Well, Senator Gillibrand, thank you so much for joining us here at Solana Policy Day. It's been a really exciting day with a ton of great leaders, but I am so excited to be sitting here talking to you. You really have been, I think, among Democratic senators, the first and finest. You were one of our first supporters, I think, when it was kind of scarce in the Democratic Party on who was on our team. But with your help, that number has grown and continues to grow, and you've been an incredibly important legislator when it comes to crypto policy. As a former securities lawyer, I'm sure you're the most fun person at a cocktail party, but you really do have what I think is an incredibly deep understanding of the technology and of our aims for the technology. You also currently serve as the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. So you really are leading the way for Democrats to take back the Senate and in that process have really been a champion for us as well on making sure that everyone understands when they come into Congress that crypto is a very important thing to us. In a Senate Democratic caucus formerly dominated by the anti crypto army and Senator Elizabeth Warren, your leadership on the issue has been a breath of fresh air and we are truly grateful to have you there. To start, can you share what drew you to this space originally and why you've made crypto policy such a priority in your agenda?
speaker: A

text: So the first time I ever heard about cryptocurrency or blockchain was from my son when he was about 12 years old. And because he was a gamer, this was a important part of the ecosystem that he was in, and I didn't understand anything about it. But over the years that followed, I became more and more interested. And when some mutual friends of mine were very much immersed in this space, I sat down with them and really learned the industry. At the same time, I met Cynthia Lummis. And Cynthia told me that she was trying to write the first market structure bill for cryptocurrency. And I said, I would love to partner with you and work on that. So we've been working as a team for the past three years on market structure. We've also wrote a stablecoin bill, which is now part of the bill that is going through Congress. So we are very excited about the work that we are doing and happy to be in this space.
speaker: B

text: Well, you said it, not me, the elephant in the room, the stablecoin bill. Thank you so much for your work. On that you introduced along with Senator Hagerty, Senator Scott and Lummis. You've really created an incredible bipartisan product that we are really excited about. The Solano ecosystem, as all of you know, uses stablecoins in countless transactions and applications to utilize the stability to transfer the value across chain. Could you share with the audience what is really inside this legislation? Kind of get under the hood and tell us why this is impactful for Solana's developers, for the projects and for users?
speaker: A

text: Well, the reason why this stablecoin bill is so important is because there are millions and millions of users across the globe and there's already been issued over $200 billion of US dollar backed stablecoins. We have domestic participants, we have foreign participants, but there's no real rules of the road. And so what this bill does is lay out who you have to be if you want to be an issuer in the United States, what rules you have to follow if you want to be a federal issuer, what rules you have to follow if you want to be a state issuer, and then what rules you have to follow if you are a foreign issuer who wants to sell those stablecoins in the United States. Now the simplicity of this bill is that anybody who issues in the United States is going to be treated as a financial services company. Our financial services laws are really clear. They have to follow the bank Secrecy Act. We have know your customer anti money laundering requirements. If you're going to be a foreign issuer and want to sell in the United States, you have to show that your jurisdiction has the same protections that we have in this jurisdiction. And those protections are important because they are trying to create financial stability across the entire ecosystem of financial services. And so this is a very good place to start on how you create a system where consumers are going to be protected that they know when they buy a stablecoin it's one to $1 backed. And that when you have an account that is holding that dollar for you to issue that stablecoin that that account has know your customer and anti money laundering requirements that that account is safe and sound under US Banking laws and trust laws. And so it just makes the system so much more reliable. So when a person's deciding which stablecoin do I want to buy, they might decide, well, I really like the safety and soundness of the US Banking system. I like the fact that this new bill requires all these protections for consumers. I want to buy a US dollar backed stablecoin that's issued in the United states that's going to create dollar dominance. Ultimately, it creates stability in our financial services industry, and it creates a set of rules that people can follow and know that they are protected from scammers and grifters who are trying to steal their money from other jurisdictions or from other places.
speaker: B

text: One of the incredible things about the Solana blockchain is how fast it reaches consensus. You can't say that about Congress. You've played an incredible role in brokering what I think is a. Is a very tenuous negotiation that's happened over the past months and weeks. And you've navigated building what I think is a really great bipartisan product. All of this happening against the backdrop of Senator Warren's war on crypto and the Trump family's foray into the technology. What lessons have you learned about building bipartisan consensus on these issues?
speaker: A

text: So I can just certainly start by saying Trump being involved in this industry is the worst news ever for this industry. I can't overstate how disruptive his activities have been because largely what he's been doing is illegal. When President Trump issues a meme coin and he invites investors from all over the globe, from foreign adversaries to countries and people and businesses that want to influence him, he is breaking the emoluments clause of the Constitution. It is illegal 100%. And so when he says he wants to start a cryptocurrency industry and he wants to have a stablecoin, he should have no involvement in that business, because if he does again, he may well break the emoluments clause. It's illegal for members of Congress, for our senior members of administration, to be able to create some business opportunity where they're going to make money off any type of consumer or any type of constituent where they can sell their office. That law should apply to President Trump. It should apply to his senior Cabinet members and the entire Congress. And so when he gets involved, it undermines the legitimacy and the strength of this industry. So it is not good news. However. However, I am somebody who works every day in Congress on a bipartisan basis to try to solve problems for my state, to try to help people in my state on every level, for all sorts of things. And so I always work on a bipartisan basis. Every piece of legislation I've ever written, I've started with a strong Republican ally to build consensus from the beginning. And so when Cynthia and I started talking about cryptocurrency and blockchain and market structure framework, we realized that stablecoin was perhaps the simplest of Everything that we were doing, perhaps the lowest hanging fruit. And so when we got involved with Senator Hagerty, who was going to be the lead on stablecoins, we started negotiating from day one about the things that we thought created safety and soundness, things that we thought would create stability in the industry, things that would protect our community banks, that would protect the state regulatory structures, that would protect consumer protection laws on both the federal and state level to make sure our consumers were protected. And so we've really enjoyed working together as a collaborative group. Angela also Brooks, who's one of the newest members of the Senate Banking Committee. She joined our coalition of negotiators, and over time, we added Ruben Gallego and Mark Warner as well. And so together, the six of us really worked hard towards building this consensus to get everyone and every stakeholder heard so we could build the best set of laws that we possibly could conceive of. And so I'm really proud of the work we've done.
speaker: B

text: That's fantastic, and thank you for work on that. To pivot now to other major legislation on the Horizon for the 119th Congress, builders are desperate for clear answers to questions as simple as, is what I'm building a security or a commodity? Can I build this in the United States, or should I build this in a more friendly jurisdiction? With current bipartisan momentum in the Senate, do you think we have an opportunity to get market structure legislation done? And if so, what timeline are we talking about here?
speaker: A

text: So I'm optimistic that if we have a large negotiating group like we just had five or six senators working together from the beginning to write a market structure bill, that we can come up with a very good bipartisan framework. I think it's very important to have a process to know when you're offering a digital asset, whether it's a digital security or a digital commodity. A lot of current law can be looked at to figure that out. If you are a centralized company that is issuing something akin to a stock, and the value of that asset goes up or down based on how well you're managing your company, how well, or how good the service you're offering is, that will typically be seen as a security because it's consistent with current law. It's called the Howey Test. If what you're offering is very decentralized, there is no centralized authority that's deciding what and how something's being offered or issued or the price, that is much more like a commodity. So that would be treated as a digital commodity. And so our legislation hopefully will Align with those two basic principles so it's easier, easy for innovators and investors and companies to know how and who their primary regulator will be. I also think there will be ways to begin to look at defi. Defi is probably the hardest thing to figure out. How do you regulate it? Because a lot of defi doesn't have any centralized management or a board or a CEO or a committee that's in charge. And as a consequence, it's very hard to assess who's in charge and how do you attribute liability. And so defi is going to be the really most, I think, difficult and challenging intellectual exercise about how do you regulate a protocol that sits on the Internet forever to be used and updated by multiple parties at all times. It's a very different idea that we don't really have a great parallel in the non digital world. Most things you have a parallel to begin to think about, but defi doesn't really have a parallel. We might start looking at property law, we might start looking at infrastructure. It's an interesting concept. And so that is going to be the challenge of the bill. But I'm very optimistic that the rest of the bill, which Cynthia and I have a draft of that we've had for a couple of years, we have a place to start to work from defi.
speaker: B

text: So I'll pivot away from legislation. Now. In addition to your hard work that you do legislating, you also have a key role leading the Democratic effort to retake the Senate majority. For folks in this room who may be pro crypto, who might be Democrat, but are nervous about the Democratic Party and the role that Elizabeth Warren's anti crypto army plays in it, what is your case to the crypto voter for supporting Dems in upcoming elections?
speaker: A

text: So I would just suggest that in this election, it's about what kind of country do you want? And I think President Trump has done some things that are very alarming to the American people. I think taking money out of Medicaid is very damaging. To have 8.6 million less people be able to get their health care through Medicaid is very alarming. People who are on Medicare are people with disabilities, seniors, veterans and children, and pregnant women. So we need health care in this country. And when you are literally taking away health care for those Medicaid recipients because you want tax breaks for the uber wealthy, it's just morally wrong and it's unfair and it doesn't represent our values as a nation. Similarly, when President Trump attack Social Security, Social Security is our money. So when you put your little bit of money in your Social Security, every paycheck you get, you don't expect it to be robbed, to give tax benefits to the ultra wealthy. And so I think people are looking at this next election as a way to create oversight and accountability over the Trump administration. I think they want a balance of power. They don't want one party to have all levers of power, because when you have all levers of power, you often overreach and the harms that are caused are real and substantial. So I think many voters are going to be looking for that balance of power to be restored. And I will be working on that with really great candidates in a lot of red and purple states. They will be moderates. They will be people who understand red and purple America well. They will be people who understand the challenges that people face every day. And they'll understand why some people voted for President Trump because they wanted a change, they wanted a disruption, they wanted things done differently. And they will understand that. And not only will they not criticize that, they will offer their own solutions and their own vision for how they would fix those problems that those voters wanted fixed. So I'm optimistic that in this election, we will have a dozen or so very strong candidates running in red and purple states who will offer a better vision for America, especially for their states, especially when it comes to these economic issues. When tariffs keep going up and down because President Trump doesn't have a clear vision about the economy, it results in businesses having to raise their prices and people not being able to afford their food or their housing or their medicine. And so those are the type of issues that these races are going to depend on. And just to defend my colleague, Senator Warren, we have a great relationship. She is a very kind and thoughtful person who cares deeply about her constituents and deeply about the world. We just disagree about this industry and how to regulate it. But she is a very thoughtful and kind person who I enjoy working with on all the other issues we work on.
speaker: B

speaker: A

text: How can the Solana community most effectively engage with legislators like yourself?
speaker: A

text: So the really important thing I would suggest is just be heard. Come to Washington, ask to meet with your member of Congress. Ask to meet with your senator, especially if you have businesses in their state or in their district. Most members of Congress want to meet their constituents. They want to know what you care about and why you care about it. And I would just suggest that this industry is so new, it's so sophisticated and complex. Not everybody gets elected to come to Congress because they're a securities lawyer. No, like, none of them do. Like, they tend to be farmers or the small business owners or moms in tennis shoes. There's all these different reasons why people want to serve in Congress, but rarely is it because they're super smart when it comes to banking and securities legislation. So I would just give them a beat. Give them time to learn your industry, learn what you're doing and why, who your customers are. One of the most exciting things about blockchain is that it, and especially as it's used in financial services, is that it democratizes finance. It opens up access to capital around the globe. And your last speaker just mentioned her friends in Afghanistan and how most people have a wallet, they do not have a bank account. And for millions of Americans who are unbanked or underbanked, this is how they can buy things, it's how they can invest things, it's how they can have ownership of their resources without predatory lending or predatory fees every time they want to send money to a loved one or participate in the financial world. And so I would just suggest, please make yourselves available. Understand people don't have the knowledge base that you do in this industry and to give them time to learn it, because they want to serve their constituents. And as their constituents, you matter to them.
speaker: B

text: So I want to close with an open ended question. You've put in a ton of work to get a variety of pieces of legislation on this topic done. You're expending political capital, you're doing the hard work of pushing back on misinformation and promoting the positive characteristics and qualities of this industry. New York has long been the financial capital of the world. How do you think effective crypto policies will impact New Yorkers for years to come?
speaker: A

text: So one of the reasons why I got involved in this space was because I want to make sure New York stays the center of the world financial markets. And we have a lot of innovators here, we have a lot of stakeholders here, we have a lot of businesses based here. In fact, New York City, Brooklyn is vying for supremacy over Silicon Valley in many respects because we want our tech businesses to locate here. And so one of the reasons why I wanted to be a leader is so I could understand what our stakeholders are trying to do, what their business models involve, making sure that this doesn't destroy access to regular finance so that you have people who can continue to regulate, to go to a community bank and get a mortgage or get a loan for their small business that is not a business that a lot of the blockchain innovators are in. And so we want to make sure we have all financial services being vibrant and successful and growing in the United States and in New York. And so I feel really proud that I've spent the time and effort to learn this industry so that it can compete worldwide. So, so that our innovators and our entrepreneurs can thrive here in the United States and know ultimately that we can out compete foreign participants because our laws are better, our laws are more reliable, and our legal system is a stronger legal system in that regard. We can then move our markets towards our platforms and our businesses because we can offer better financial services and better structure in our regulatory protections for consumers.
